title: Establishing context-aware reference values for the blood count in the 21st century
summary:
In medicine, certain blood measurements (blood reference values) are important to distinguish between normal and abnormal or healthy and sick. The existing reference values are ranges based on safety values of healthy individuals collected from a broad population. Individuals with values outside these ranges are considered sick and lead to further testing or treatment.
However, in a diverse population there can be problems:
1. readings from sick people could be misclassified as normal.
2. readings from healthy people who do not fit well with the group used to establish the reference values could be misclassified as abnormal and diseased, leading to unnecessary testing and treatment.
It has already been established that women often have lower hemoglobin levels compared to men. The hemoglobin level shows how much hemoglobin is present in the blood. It is an important component of red blood cells. In addition, moderate to severe anemia has been detected more frequently in women. 

Another important aspect is that around 30% of women have an iron deficiency in their blood. This reference value for ferritin in the blood is often not recognized because the currently valid reference value mainly applies to men. Ferritin helps the body to store iron. Interestingly, it was found that women benefited from iron treatment even though their hemoglobin levels were actually normal. This suggests that iron deficiency plays an important role even in apparently normal hemoglobin levels. Current data on this topic is still very limited in Germany. 

Another point that has attracted attention concerns neutrophil granulocytes in the blood. Neutrophil granulocytes are a type of white blood cell that help the body fight disease. In healthy women, the neutrophil granulocyte count was more variable than in men. This means that women are more likely to be incorrectly diagnosed with an increase or decrease in these blood cells. This could lead to unnecessary diagnostic measures or treatments, such as the administration of antibiotics. 

In addition to gender, there is another factor that influences the reference range for neutrophil granulocytes. This is the so-called Duffy antigen status. This is a characteristic on the red blood cells that is present in some people and not in others. It can affect certain blood values and is also important to better understand how the body reacts to certain diseases. People with the Duffy-null type have a lower level of neutrophils in their blood. The reference range for the Duffy zero type should therefore be adjusted, but this has not yet happened. In Germany, it is also not yet known how many people have this Duffy zero type and in which groups it is particularly common, as this has never been investigated.

Overall, it is clear that incorrect reference values for iron and granulocytes can lead to both inadequate detection of iron deficiency and incorrect diagnoses.
The aim of this study is to review these blood reference values and, if necessary, to initiate an adjustment.
conditions: healthy persons (without diseases with any influence on blood values)

interventions.name:
All parameters are recorded at the same time

Laboratory parameters measured on healthy persons:
Blood count, small
Differential blood count
Creatinine
ferritin
CRP
iron
transferrin
Transferrin saturation
GOT
GPT
Gamma-GT
Duffy genotyping

Questionnaires collected:
DiMIS-DiVersO2

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
-Sufficient knowledge of German to understand the study and to give informed consent
-Willingness and ability to give informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
-Known chronic illness that is highly likely to lead to relevant blood count changes (e.g. chronic lymphocytic leukemia, anemia)
-Blood donation / blood transfusions within the last 3 months
-Pregnancy or breastfeeding (fully breastfeeding for the last 6 months)
-Current infection (e.g. cold, tonsillitis, appendicitis), fever or CRP >5mg/dl
-Known chronic infectious diseases such as HIV infection or hepatitis B, C or D, syphilis, haemoparasites or intestinal parasite infection
